```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

```

## Dataset 1 - Populous States

```{r}

library(tidyverse)

population <- read_csv("census_top10_states_2022_untidy.csv")

head(population)
glimpse(population)


```

```{r}

# Convert population data from wide to long format
population_long <- population %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(Rank, `Geographic Area`),
    names_to = "Year",
    values_to = "Population"
  )

# View 
head(population_long)

```

```{r}

# Calculate population changes from 2020 to 2022
population_change <- population_long %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(
    "April 1, 2020 (Estimates Base)",
    "July 1, 2022"
  )) %>%
  select(`Geographic Area`, Year, Population) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Year,
    values_from = Population
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Population_Change = `July 1, 2022` -
      `April 1, 2020 (Estimates Base)`,
    Percent_Change = round(
      Population_Change /
        `April 1, 2020 (Estimates Base)` * 100, 2
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Percent_Change))

# Display results
print(population_change)

# Display all columns
print(population_change, width = Inf)


```

## Results & Conclusions

After changing the populace data from wide to long, I computed the population changes for the top 10 most populous states between April 2020 and July 2022.

Florida had the greatest percent increase with 3.28%, rigth before Texas at 3.03%. However, Texas had the biggest numerical increase, getting about 884,000 residents.

New York seemed to have experienced the biggest percent decrease at 2.59 %, which equated to a loss of 524,000 residents. California and illinois also faced apparent population declines.

## Dataset 2: US Average Tuition (2004–2016)

```{r}

# Dataset 2: US Average Tuition

tuition <- read_csv("us_avg_tuition(Table 5).csv")

# Inspect the dataset
head(tuition)
glimpse(tuition)

# Check missing values
colSums(is.na(tuition))


names(tuition)


```

```{r}

# Transform from wide to long format
tuition_long <- tuition %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -State,
    names_to = "Academic_Year",
    values_to = "Tuition"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Tuition = readr::parse_number(as.character(Tuition))
  )

# Check transformed data
head(tuition_long)

# Average tuition by state across all years
state_avg <- tuition_long %>%
  group_by(State) %>%
  summarise(
    Average_Tuition = round(mean(Tuition, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Average_Tuition))

print(state_avg, n = 10)

# Highest tuition states in 2015-16
highest_tuition <- tuition_long %>%
  filter(Academic_Year == "2015-16") %>%
  arrange(desc(Tuition))

print(head(highest_tuition, 10))

# Compare tuition in the first and last years
tuition_change <- tuition_long %>%
  filter(Academic_Year %in% c("2004-05", "2015-16")) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Academic_Year,
    values_from = Tuition
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Change = `2015-16` - `2004-05`,
    Percent_Change = round(Change / `2004-05` * 100, 2)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Percent_Change))

print(tuition_change, n = 10)

# Average tuition across states by academic year
yearly_tuition <- tuition_long %>%
  group_by(Academic_Year) %>%
  summarise(
    Average_Tuition = mean(Tuition, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot tuition trends
ggplot(yearly_tuition,
       aes(x = Academic_Year, y = Average_Tuition, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Average US Tuition, 2004-2016",
    x = "Academic Year",
    y = "Average Tuition ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

```{r}

head(state_avg, 5)
head(tuition_change, 5)
tail(tuition_change, 5)

```

## Results & Conclusions

After transforming the tuition dataset from wide to long, I was able to compare every state's tuition throughout academic years.

Seeing the results, Iowa faced a 15.62% increase between 2004-05 and 2015-16, while Missouri went up by 14.54% and Montana went up by 12.81%. Maryland also saw an upwards of 7.41%.

Ohio showcased a 1.75% decrease over the same period. This insinuates that tuiton trends were not uniform throughout the states.

## Dataset 3: Business Costs and Revenue

```{r}

# Dataset 3: Business Costs and Revenue

business <- read_csv("5A_BusinessCostsRevenue.csv")

# Inspect structure
head(business)
names(business)
glimpse(business)

```

```{r}

# Standardize column names
business_clean <- business %>%
  rename(
    Jan_Cost = `Jan Cost`,
    Jan_Revenue = `Jan Revenue`,
    Feb_Cost = `Feb Cost (k)`,
    Feb_Revenue = `Feb Revenue`,
    March_Cost = `March Cost (k)`,
    March_Revenue = `March Revenue`,
    April_Cost = April_Cost,
    April_Revenue = April_revenue,
    May_Cost = `May Cost`,
    May_Revenue = `may revenue`,
    June_Cost = `June Cost`,
    June_Revenue = `June Revenue`
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Feb_Cost = Feb_Cost * 1000,
    March_Cost = March_Cost * 1000
  )

# Convert wide data into long format
business_long <- business_clean %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(Location, Name),
    names_to = c("Month", ".value"),
    names_sep = "_"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Month = factor(
      Month,
      levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "March",
                 "April", "May", "June")
    ),
    Profit = Revenue - Cost
  )

# Inspect transformed data
print(business_long, n = 30)

```

```{r}


# Calculate monthly business performance
monthly_summary <- business_long %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Cost = sum(Cost, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_Revenue = sum(Revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_Profit = sum(Profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(monthly_summary)


```

## Results & Conclusions

After cleaning the business dataset via standardization of column names and dollar conversions across february and March, I was able to restructure the data into long form and compute profits by reducing costs from revenue.

The results show that January produced 50,000 in profit, then came March with 49,000 and February with 43,000. April was the single month with a staggering loss of 22,000.

The sudden profit gain of 6, 145, 000 in May showed an unusual turnout that may need to be studied before coming towards conclusive business decision.

Ultimately, reshaping the dataset facilitated the process of comparing monthly performance and pinpont unusual observations that can affect analysis.
